observed_mechanics: 0x00bb9b00 CMP byte ptr [ESP+0x8],0x0 is the only selector test and it is a byte compare, so any non-zero value of the third argument takes the set path.
0x00bb9b05 JZ 0x00bb9b11 is the sole branch; the two paths are disjoint and each is three instructions long.

0x00bb9b07/0x00bb9b0b load the mask into EAX and OR it into the memory operand. Because the OR's destination is memory, this is a genuine read-modify-write of the field, not a blind store of the mask.

0x00bb9b11/0x00bb9b15/0x00bb9b17 load the mask into EDX, complement it, and AND it into the same memory operand. The NOT is applied to the MASK register only; the field is never inverted, so bits outside the mask are preserved in both directions.

Both exits are RET 0x8, so the callee pops exactly two words on either path and the caller's stack is unchanged on return. There is no PUSH, no SUB ESP and no register save in the body: the function is a leaf that cannot spill and does not need to.
ECX is read at 0x00bb9b0b and 0x00bb9b17 and is never written, so the receiver cannot be clobbered by the argument loads into EAX and EDX.
0x00bb9b00 appears nowhere in .rdata or .data as a dword (scan total=0), so it is a non-virtual member and its class is not vtable-proven.

sibling_analysis.question: how does this relate to the SDK's cStarRecord::SetFlag at 0x00bb9c70?
sibling_analysis.answer: They are different functions with different contracts. 0x00bb9c70 takes one argument, compares it against 0x3e4353b (cStarRecord::TYPE) and 0x179c807, and returns this AND (arg != 0x179c807); it never touches +0x5c. 0x00bb9b00 takes a mask and a selector and read-modify-writes +0x5c. semantic_contract: Given a star record, this function sets or clears an arbitrary subset of the bits of a single 32-bit flag word held at receiver offset +0x5c. 1. It reads the selector argument as a byte and compares it with zero (0x00bb9b00). Any non-zero value means set. 2. On the set path it ORs the mask into the flag word in memory, which preserves every bit outside the mask (0x00bb9b07, 0x00bb9b0b). 3. On the clear path it complements the mask in a register and ANDs that into the flag word, so only the masked bits are cleared and the field itself is never inverted (0x00bb9b11, 0x00bb9b15, 0x00bb9b17). 4. Both paths return with RET 0x8, so the callee pops its two stack words and the caller's stack is unchanged. Invariants: the operation is idempotent for a zero mask in both directions; it is not a blind store, so concurrent independent flag updates to different bits compose; the function reads no global, calls nothing, saves no register, and is therefore a leaf that can never fail or have an observable side effect outside that one dword.
classification_rationale: The complete 29-byte body, the ABI, the single field offset, the branch polarity, the constants and the empty callee and global sets were all read directly from the disassembly, and three separate caller windows show real masks including two the SDK does not document. It is not STRONG_SEMANTIC because: (a) OWNING CLASS AND FIELD NAME - the function is non-virtual and appears in no vtable, so cStarRecord::mFlags is an offset-based candidate; (b) the method has no SDK name, and the SDK's only declared flag setter is a different function at a different address, so the reconstructed name is a label; (c) the per-bit semantics are not established: cStarRecord.h documents 0x1, 0x2, 0x10 and 0x1000 and speculates about 0x8, 0x40 and 0x200, while the inspected callers additionally exercise 0x4, 0x8000 and 0x40000000, so at least three live bits have no documented meaning; and (d) 21 of the 24 canonical callers were not disassembled, so the set of masks actually used in the shipping game is only partially sampled.
semantic_findings: The function is a pure bitfield setter with a byte selector. Its whole observable effect is one OR or one AND on a single dword.

The NOT is applied to the mask register, not to the field. An implementation that cleared by ANDing with the complement of the STORED value would be wrong, and this one is not: bits outside the mask survive both directions.
The selector is compared as a byte, so it accepts any non-zero value, not just 1. The caller at 0x00bb569f passes a runtime boolean, which is consistent with that.

The function saves no register and calls nothing, which is only possible because ECX is never written and the two argument temporaries are EAX and EDX. It is the cheapest possible member and is used in bulk: 0x00bb4f30 calls it once per entry of a dword table to clear bit 30 across a whole list.

The inspected callers use masks that match cStarRecord.h's StarFlags for 0x1 and 0x2 and then diverge: 0x4, 0x8000 and 0x40000000 are set or cleared by shipping code but are absent from the header, so the header's flag list is incomplete. That is a correction to the SDK, not merely a gap in this analysis.

The function is called from 0x00fe9580 and 0x00c5f770 as well as from the galaxy code, so the flag word is mutated from presentation and gameplay code outside cStarManager, which means the field is shared state rather than a private cache.
unresolved_questions: What do bits 2, 15 and 30 mean? They are set or cleared by shipping callers but are undocumented in cStarRecord.h, and their names cannot be recovered statically.

What do bits 3, 6 and 9 mean? cStarRecord.h speculates in comments about 0x8 (monolith), 0x40 (destroyed planet) and 0x200 (raid), but no inspected caller of this function exercises them, so the speculation is untested here.

Is the +0x5c word shared with any other structure? cStarRecord.h places mFlags there, and the SDK's own TODO comment at cStarRecord.h:105 reads 'TODO 1 << 4 (16) is visited? sub_BB8B50', which suggests the reverse engineer was themselves unsure about this field's flag discipline.

Do all 24 callers use only single-bit masks? The three inspected windows pass 0x1, 0x2, 0x4, 0x8000 and 0x40000000, all single-bit, but 0x00bb4f30's loop passes the SAME mask for every entry while loading a different dword from the table into ECX's target field via the callee - so the per-entry value is read but not used as a mask. That inconsistency is unexplained and the remaining callers were not checked.
Is the function ever called with a mask of 0? That would be a no-op in both directions, and no inspected caller does it, but nothing in the code forbids it.

Which cStarManager member is 0x00bb5640? The SDK symbol table places cStarManager::RecordToPlanet at 0x00BB5B50 and StarGenerationMessageHandler at 0x00BB5F00, so 0x00bb5640 is an unnamed member of the same class, and it is the caller that exercises three of the five masks.
runtime_gates: No original-process trace exists for 0x00bb9b00; every claim is static.

A runtime trace would be needed to observe the actual flag word of a real star record before and after a state transition, and to confirm that no other code path writes +0x5c outside this function and the two siblings that read it.
The undocumented bit meanings can only be resolved by correlating runtime flag values with game events, which no recorded run provides.
